desc:
For every inversion, a pair of indices i < j with nums[i] > nums[j], define its distance as j - i. Return the sum of the distances of all inversions, modulo 1,000,000,007.

nums = [3, 1, 2]     inversions (0,1) distance 1 and (0,2) distance 2  -> 3
nums = [2, 2, 1, 1]  (0,2) 2, (0,3) 3, (1,2) 1, (1,3) 2           -> 8
nums = [1, 2, 3]     -> 0
constraints: Values may repeat; equal values never form an inversion
hints: Listing the inversions is O(n<sup>2</sup>) in the worst case. Group them by the right index j instead: the contribution of all inversions ending at j is a simple expression.

For a fixed j, let S be the set of earlier indices i with nums[i] > nums[j]. Their total distance is |S| * j - (sum of the indices in S). So you need both a count and a sum of indices for 'earlier and larger'.

Compress the values to ranks and keep two Fenwick trees over ranks: one storing counts and one storing index sums. Querying the suffix (ranks above the current one) gives both numbers for each j in O(log n).
editorial: Sweep j from left to right and imagine all earlier elements inserted into a structure keyed by value rank. The inversions that end at j are the earlier elements with a strictly larger value. If there are c of them with index sum s, their distances add up to c * j - s.

So we need, for a rank threshold, the count and the index sum of the elements above it. Two Fenwick trees do this: one adds 1 at the element's rank, the other adds its index. The values above rank r equal the total inserted so far minus the prefix up to r. Accumulate the sum with big or 64-bit integers and reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 at the end (the exact sum can reach about n<sup>3</sup>/6, around 8.5 × 10<sup>10</sup> here, which is more than 32 bits).
Time O(n log n), space O(n). A merge-sort version also works: carry the sum of original indices along with each sorted element.
solution:
def inversionDistanceSum(nums):
    M = 1000000007
    vals = sorted(set(nums))
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
    m = len(vals)
    cnt = [0] * (m + 1)
    idx = [0] * (m + 1)
    total = 0
    seen = 0
    seen_idx = 0
    for j, x in enumerate(nums):
        r = rank[x]
        k = r
        c = 0
        s = 0
        while k > 0:
            c += cnt[k]
            s += idx[k]
            k -= k & -k
        greater_cnt = seen - c
        greater_idx = seen_idx - s
        total += greater_cnt * j - greater_idx
        k = r
        while k <= m:
            cnt[k] += 1
            idx[k] += j
            k += k & -k
        seen += 1
        seen_idx += j
    return total % M
